Hatchlings of Kuroiwa emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a total length of 2.4 centimeters [Lb = 2.4 centimeters], reflecting the modest size typical of many gekkotan neonates. After the hatching event, these young individuals immediately begin a period of rapid mass gain, fueled by the progressive yolk utilization that characterizes the first days of exogenous feeding. When maintained under stable thermal conditions in captivity, specifically a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the incubation interval from oviposition to eclosion is approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days], a duration that aligns well with values recorded for other subtropical Goniurosaurus species. This relatively short incubation period, combined with the small neonatal size, suggests a reproductive strategy that prioritizes rapid development over large offspring size, a pattern that may confer advantages in the predator-dense karst ecosystems the species inhabits. The embryonated egg, heavily dependent on its yolk reserves, undergoes cleavage and gastrulation before the shell pipping event signals the commencement of emergence.

Juveniles grow steadily as they transition into the sub-adult phase, with sexual maturation in females occurring once the total length at puberty is achieved at 7.5 centimeters [Lp = 7.5 centimeters]. This morphological benchmark marks the onset of gonadal activation and the ability to produce a first egg clutch, though the exact age at this transition can exhibit some variability depending on local resource availability. Adult body size in this species is strikingly dimorphic: females ultimately attain a larger total length, reaching about 9.58 centimeters [Li = about 9.58 centimeters], whereas males cap their growth at a more modest 9.02 centimeters [Li = 9.02 centimeters]. This reversed size dimorphism, uncommon among geckos, may be linked to fecundity selection, as a larger female body cavity can accommodate a greater clutch volume. The maximum recorded adult wet weight for the species is 20.18 grams [Wwi = 20.18 grams], a value that underscores the relatively lightweight build of these scansorial reptiles, an adaptation that facilitates movement across the vertical limestone surfaces they inhabit.

Reproductive output in Kuroiwa has been characterized under controlled captive conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], with females producing clutches that consistently contain two eggs [N_R_i = clutches that consistently contain two eggs]. Field surveys and captive breeding records further indicate that individual females typically produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], a rate that is relatively low compared to many tropical geckos but likely constrained by the seasonal availability of invertebrate prey in their subtropical island habitat. This annual reproductive rate, calculated from the product of clutch size and clutch frequency, suggests that maximum annual fecundity is modest, with each reproductively active adult contributing only four offspring per year. The pairing of a small clutch size with infrequent nesting events aligns with the life history profile of a species that appears to invest heavily in each offspring, as indicated by the relatively large egg size for the body mass of the female.

Longevity data from both wild-caught and captive individuals suggest a remarkably extended lifespan for a gecko of this body size, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately seven years [am = approximately seven years] when kept at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan of around 2,555 days is considerably longer than what has been reported for many similarly sized gekkonids, which often senesce after only two to three years. The extended reproductive window afforded by such longevity allows females to accumulate multiple breeding seasons, potentially compensating for the low annual fecundity by spreading reproductive effort over many years. Natural mortality in the wild is likely driven by predation from introduced mammals and snakes on the Ryukyu Islands, as well as by the frequent typhoons that scour the karst outcrops, though the species' cryptic coloration and nocturnal habits provide some protection. Reproductive senescence, when it eventually occurs, appears as a gradual decline in clutch viability rather than an abrupt cessation of egg production.

Comparative analyses with other members of the genus Goniurosaurus reveal that Kuroiwa occupies a somewhat intermediate position in terms of body size and reproductive pace. The total length at birth of 2.4 centimeters [Lb = 2.4 centimeters] is comparable to that of Goniurosaurus luii, yet the ultimate female length of 9.58 centimeters [Li = 9.58 centimeters] is notably smaller than that of the much larger Goniurosaurus hainanensis. The timing of sexual maturation at 7.5 centimeters [Lp = 7.5 centimeters] total length suggests that females begin allocating resources toward reproduction well before they attain their asymptotic size, a pattern common among squamates that continue growing throughout life. The relatively high adult mass of 20.18 grams [Wwi = 20.18 grams] for its length indicates a robust body condition, possibly an adaptation for storing energy during the cooler months when prey becomes scarce in the subtropical winter. The maximum lifespan of seven years [am = seven years] under stable captive conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] places it among the longer-lived members of its genus, a trait that may reflect the low extrinsic mortality rates encountered in the absence of their primary predators.
